wa_clamshell_cave_climbs.blurb: A small crag beside Icicle Creek outside Leavenworth, on the east slope of the Cascades. The mix is unusual for a roadside wall: roughly a dozen trad lines, a handful of bolted sport routes, a top-rope option and a few boulder problems from V0 to V2. Roped climbs are mostly moderate, from 5.7 into the 5.10s, with one 5.11, so it suits climbers building up their crack skills. Most lines finish at fixed anchors, but a small rack is worth bringing. A tier of shorter routes sits just above the main wall. It is a good pick for a short day when you want variety rather than a single style.

wa_b_canopy_crag.blurb: One of the climbing walls on Little Si, just outside North Bend and a short drive from Seattle. Canopy is a sport-only cliff of about 50 feet, and it is steeper on the grade than its height suggests. Of its two dozen routes, most fall in the 5.11 and 5.12 range, with a few at 5.13 and only a scattering of easier climbs from 5.6 to 5.10, so it is a better fit for experienced leaders than for newcomers. Routes are sustained and the holds can be shaped by wear. Many lines wander away from their anchors, so lowering off while clipping draws is the usual advice. Of the Little Si walls, it has one of the quicker walks in.

wa_roadside_rock_west.blurb: The west-facing side of Roadside Rock, a granite outcrop on the Banks Lake shoreline in central Washington. Nearly all of its two dozen routes are bolted sport lines, plus a single trad route. Difficulty clusters in the 5.9 and 5.10 range, with a handful of easier lines at 5.7 and 5.8 and one 5.12, which makes it friendly for climbers stepping up from moderates. Some lines rise straight from the water, and you can reach the rock by boat or on foot around the south end, where a scramble through ledges leads toward the upper tiers. Summers here run hot, so spring and autumn are the comfortable times.

wa_kotick_memorial_wall.blurb: A short basalt wall in Echo Basin, the small coulee next to Frenchman Coulee at Vantage on the Columbia River. About a dozen bolted sport lines share the wall with ten crack and trad routes, and nearly all of it is moderate: a few climbs at 5.5 to 5.7, a solid middle at 5.8 and 5.9, and the hardest routes at 5.10. That puts it among the gentler walls in the basin, handy for newer leaders or for a warm-up before the steeper pillars nearby. The walls tend to be sunny and have some shelter from wind. The walk from the Sunshine Wall approach is brief.

wa_cliff_drive.blurb: A small basalt cliff right in Spokane, close enough for an after-work session. Most of the roughly two dozen routes are bolted and short, with a few set up for top-roping from anchors above. Grades run from 5.6 to 5.11, with the bulk at 5.7 through 5.10, so it works for beginners leading their first bolted routes as well as for climbers wanting a quick pump. Six quickdraws are generally plenty. The Main Wall holds the most lines, and a smaller formation just downhill has a few more. Expect a city setting with views over downtown from the top, and some litter in the trees below.
wa_cliff_drive.approach: A very short walk, about a block or two, from the road along a steep path between the rocks.

wa_deception_wall.blurb: The tallest face among the Exit 38 crags off I-90 near North Bend, set above the old railroad grade. All 23 routes are bolted sport climbs, mostly 40 to 60 feet, though several run past 100 feet and carry mid-route rappel anchors. The grades start to bite early: a few at 5.7 and 5.9, then a heavy cluster from 5.10 through 5.11, and a short run of harder lines up to the 5.13 and 5.14 range. The metamorphic rock varies in quality. Getting a belay can take some work, since reaching the base means descending and walking around the railbed.
wa_deception_wall.parking_note: Gravel pullouts on SE Homestead Valley Road, roughly half a mile from the Exit 38 ramp and before Change Creek. The trail leaves from across the road.

wa_gibralter_rocks.blurb: A large triangular formation in Northrup Canyon on the Banks Lake side of central Washington, with a mix that includes boulders. About thirteen boulder problems range from V0 up to V5, alongside eight bolted sport routes and two trad lines. Roped grades run from 5.8 into the low 5.12s, centered on the 5.10s. Rock quality is uneven, with some excellent stone and some poor, so test holds. The face is sunny for most of the day, while the wall at the south end keeps its shade until mid-afternoon. Bring a pad if you plan to try the canyon boulders.

wa_megadike_north.blurb: The biggest concentration of routes at The Dikes, a set of basalt fins above the North Fork Touchet River in the Blue Mountains south of Dayton. The rock forms a line of towers split by notches up a steep slope. All 23 routes are bolted, with closely spaced bolts and lengths up to roughly 120 feet. Grades are friendly: a few easy fifth-class lines, a big group at 5.8, and a handful reaching 5.10. Routes up the tower edges are usually easier than the faces. Many climbs stay shaded, which keeps it comfortable in midsummer, and you are unlikely to meet crowds.
wa_megadike_north.parking_note: From the Middle Point Ridge trailhead, drive about 1.1 to 1.2 miles further along the road to a dirt-road junction and a large pullout. The trail starts between those two parking spots.

_conflicts.wa_gibralter_rocks: Stored rock is migmatite; the page describes the formation as granite (https://mountainproject.com/area/106273148/gibralter-rocks, https://www.mountainproject.com/area/106269053/banks-lake).
